messages.subject: some utilities (promoter, array builder)
parts:
As I refactored the matrix lib, I wrote a couple of
utilities that may be useful elsewhere. Template
metaprogramming is getting easier as I get the hang of
it.

The first generalizes the to_var and assign (I'll
get around to removing those soon):

// assign f to t, promoting if necessary
void promoter<F,T>::promote(const F& f, T& t);

// return the promotion of f to type T
T promoter<F,T>::promote_to(const F& f);

This will work recursively through structured
types std::vector and Eigen::Matrix arbitrarily
nested. F and T can be any types where an F is
assignable to T (e.g., F=double, T=stan::agrad::var).

If F==T, it's a no-op.

promoter<std::vector<double>, std::vector<stan::agrad::var> >
::promote(f,t);

I second thing is a little utility function in stan/math/matrix.hpp to
help me compile array expressions. It works so that this:

std::vector<double> x
= stan::math::array_builder<double>()
.add(1.0)
.add(2.0)
.add(3.0)
.array();

is the same as:

std::vector<double> x;
x.push_back(1.0);
x.push_back(2.0);
x.push_back(3.0);

but produces the result as an expression (no
need to declare a local variable x).

It uses the builder pattern (build, chaining adds, return).
It can add anything that can be assigned to type T, recursively
through all of our types.

template <typename T>
struct array_builder {
std::vector<T> x_;
array_builder() : x_() { }
template <typename F>
array_builder& add(const F& u) {
T t;
promoter<F,T>::promote(u,t);
x_.push_back(t);
return *this;
}
std::vector<T> array() {
return x_;
}
};

In the past, I've only ever used this pattern for building immutables
with complex construction configs, but I needed it here in order to
be able to create an expression (rather than sequence of statements)
that produced a std::vector. I'll need the same thing for Eigen::Matrix
when I do matrix and vector expressions. (I'm not done with array
expressions yet -- I have about 100 places where expressions occur during
generation where I now have to distinguish parameters from data in
order to generate arrays of the appropriate type.)

- Bob
